messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: unit vectors?
parts:
I'm trying to fix unit vectors, but looking at the
actual transform definition in stan-dev/math leaves me worried:

template <typename T, int R, int C>
Eigen::Matrix<T, R, C>
unit_vector_constrain(const Eigen::Matrix<T, R, C>& y, T& lp) {
using std::sqrt;
check_vector("unit_vector_constrain", "y", y);
check_nonzero_size("unit_vector_constrain", "y", y);
const T SN = dot_self(y);
check_positive_finite("unit_vector_constrain", "norm", SN);
lp -= 0.5 * SN;
return y / sqrt(SN);
}

For one thing, this doesn't look like it'll work if R and C
are both dynamic.

But my big concern is that it's going to be unidentified on
the unconstrained space. Is there a way to do this with K-1
parameters that would be better? And is that the right log Jacobian
determinant? The (inverse) transform is from unconstrained y to
y / sqrt(SN), but that has a dense Jacobian, so I'm confused.
There's no entry in the manual chapter I can crib from, either.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] unit vectors?
parts:
No way to do this with K - 1 parameters. The problem is that
there is no isomorphism between S^{n} and R^{n - 1} because
even though the dimensions are the same the topologies are
different. Honestly I don’t like this being here at all.

There is a way to naturally apply HMC to these other topologies,
but it would require us to be be able to split the parameters by
their topologies.

We have talked about this before.

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/Tseqd6Sj-x4/esI9YED7BAAJ

It does not identify the radius, so we take the radius to be r = 1, which is also the standard deviation being used for the normal "prior" on the primitives that implies the unit vector is uniformally distributed on the surface of the hypersphere.

Wikipedia version: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere#Uniformly_at_random_from_the_.28n.C2.A0.E2.88.92.C2.A01.29-sphere
Edelman version (see section 5): http://web.mit.edu/18.325/www/handouts/handout2.pdf

Ben

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] unit vectors?
parts:
I played with this issue a while back and have some notes that I'll try to dig up.  I've been meaning to finish and publish them, so maybe this will be an incentive.

Anyway, there is a way to do this which is legit.  It involves introducing an auxiliary variable which is the norm of the unconstrained vector and giving it a density.

To be concrete (if not formal):

Unconstrained space: x \in \R^K
Constrained space: d \in S^{K+1}, r \in \R^+  (i.e., r is strictly positive)

Transformations are then:

Unconstrained -> Constrained: d = x / ||x||, r = ||x||
Constrained -> Unconstrained: x = r*d

Where r is an auxiliary variable.  Now you have a standard, invertible transformation which you can treat using change of variables just like anything else.

To ensure the distribution on x is proper we assume the user defines a (proper) posterior on d but we need a proper distribution on r.  I believe what Ben had long ago proposed (and was probably what got implemented in Stan right now, I haven't checked) is to put a N(0,1) distribution on x, and this corresponds to something like a chi distribution on r with K DoFs.  Anyway, if you do this, then you get a well defined transformation and a proper distribution on the unconstrained space.

The practical issues are:
1) We need to incorporate the distribution on r implicitly and 
2) We don't care about r and don't really want to have to keep track of it.

Issue 1 can be fixed by including the distribution over r along with the Jacobian correction.  Issue 2 is also pretty easy, since the distribution over d is invariant to r so we can discard the value of r when we transform to the constrained space and we can choose an arbitrary value for it (e.g., 1) when transform to the unconstrained space.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] unit vectors?
parts:
On Thursday, March 24, 2016 at 5:28:57 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Thanks.  Got it.  The Wikipedia article was very clear (even though
it didn't have any justification).  I think it's saying the same thing
as Marcus, with the radius being the "auxiliary" variable that gets
a unit normal distribution.

I think that is not what Marcus is saying. We only need the transformation from a unit_simplex to the unconstrained space for initial values. So, if someone gives a valid unit_simplex as an initial value, then just take r to be 1.0 and copy the unit_simplex into the "unconstrained" space. Then when the action starts, it will take the thing in the unconstrained space and divide by its Euclidean norm (which is 1.0) to create the unit_vector. Then it moves in the unconstrained space to something without a norm of 1.0 but it normalizes to form the unit vector.

We already have the unit_vector_constrain and unit_vector_free functions, but when it creates a model where a unit_vector is a parameter, it makes it too short by one element.

And I take it that it means that the "Jacobian" is really just the normal
and I don't need another Jacobian correction in there?

Right, the form of the Jacobian determinant is a product of standard normal kernels, which is implemented in log-form by unit_vector_constrain. Or equivalently, putting a standard normal prior on the unconstrained parameters implies a uniform prior on the unit_vector. It is a very similar principle to putting particular symmetric beta priors on canonical partial correlations implies a uniform prior on a correlation matrix.

Ben
